newsitem.title: MEXICO: Former Mexican president flatly denies drug links.
newsitem.headline: Former Mexican president flatly denies drug links.

text.p: Disgraced former President Carlos Salinas angrily denied press allegations over the weekend linking him and his family to top Mexican drug lords and threatened to sue those who made the charges.

Salinas, who lives in voluntary exile in Ireland, issued the denial in a statement dictated on Sunday to his lawyer. It followed the publication of Mexican press reports alleging that the former president, his father, brother Raul and sister Adriana had repeatedly met a leading drug trafficker and Raul had taken drug money in return for protecting traffickers.

"Carlos Salinas de Gortari ... categorically rejects the remarks which have supposedly been made in testimony collected by United States government authorities and which some national press media have reproduced," the statement said.
"....we have considered the need to exercise penal and civil actions in (Mexico) and abroad against those who have originated these imputations which constitute an infamy."
The statement, given to Reuters on Monday, defended Adriana and the clan's father Raul Salinas. But it did not defend the ex-president's imprisoned brother Raul by name.
Carlos Salinas has said that his brother, in jail since March 1995 on illicit enrichment and murder charges, must explain the origin of his fortune of at least $300 million.

The news weekly Proceso and left-leaning daily La Jornada both published cover stories on Sunday quoting witnesses as saying the Salinas family partied with drug lord Juan Garcia Abrego and benefited from drug money during the Salinas presidency from 1988 to 1994.

Garcia Abrego was head of Mexico's Gulf Cartel, shipping tonnes of marijuana and cocaine over the border to the United States until his arrest in January 1996. A Houston judge sentenced him to life imprisonment without parole last month.

Both Mexican news reports were allegedly based on testimony given to U.S. investigators probing the origin of $9 million owned by Mario Ruiz Massieu, a former Mexican Attorney-General now under house arrest in the U.S. Ruiz Massieu is wanted in Mexico on charges of embezzlement and obstruction of justice but has so far successfully fought off attempts by the Mexican government to have him extradited.

The U.S. Embassy was closed on Monday for a holiday and Mexican legal and government officials declined comment on the press reports. Salinas lawyer Mariano Albor was also not available for comment on the text of his client's statement.

Both Proceso and La Jornada said the explosive new testimony was collected by U.S. prosecutors as part of efforts to prove that Ruiz Massieu's fortune came from drug payoffs. They quoted a witness named Magdalena Ruiz Pelayo as saying two top politicians murdered in 1994 -- Ruiz Massieu's brother Jose Francisco and presidential candidate Luis Donaldo Colosio -- had both taken drug money as well.

While gossip about links between top members of Mexico's long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and drug traffickers has long circulated, the two news reports were a rare instance of more concrete information surfacing in a notoriously closed society.
Opposition politicians were quick to comment.

"Organized crime and drug trafficking cannot exist without the complicity of the highest levels (of authority). It is more than evident that the relationship which a group close to Carlos Salinas had with drug trafficking allowed big fortunes to be amassed," left-wing deputy Graco Ramirez told Reuters.
